GRU4Rec’s strongest directly relevant evidence favors BPR-max or cross-entropy over ordinary BPR/TOP1. BPR-max emphasizes high-scoring sampled negatives through softmax weights: −log Σⱼ softmax(r)ⱼ·sigmoid(r₊−rⱼ), plus weighted negative-score regularization. This avoids diluting gradients across many easy negatives. The official implementation also supports logQ sampling correction for cross-entropy, making sampling distribution and correction important experimental choices. [Original paper](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf), [official implementation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec).

Recent evidence cautions against assuming harder negatives improve every category or tail. A 2024 sequential-recommendation study compared random, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling across three datasets with 20 repeats: uniform sampling favored popular items; popularity-based negatives sometimes balanced popularity bands while reducing aggregate accuracy. False negatives are another concern: unobserved items can represent genuine interests, as documented by UFNRec. Its teacher-based remedy should not be imported into this single-model experiment. [2024 sampling study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276), [UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116).

Practical hypothesis: compare BPR-max against sampled softmax using the same GRU4Rec backbone and candidate budgets; separately vary uniform versus mildly popularity-weighted sampling and a limited hard-negative fraction. Exclude padding, the positive target and observed training-history items; this cannot eliminate unknown false negatives. These are proposed ablations, not established Electronics gains. Select by the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10; larger sampled margins or better lower-tail diagnostics alone do not demonstrate improvement.
